title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: On the twelfth of November, Kutuzov's army was camped outside Olmutz, preparing for a review the next day by both Emperors — Russian and Austrian. The Guards, having just arrived from Russia, spent the night ten miles away and were to march straight to the review field at Olmutz by ten the next morning.

That day, Nicholas Rostov received a letter from Boris saying that the Ismaylov regiment was camped ten miles from Olmutz for the night, and that Boris wanted to see him because he had a letter and money for him. Rostov badly needed money just then. Now that the troops were stationed near Olmutz after their active campaigning, the camp was swarming with well-stocked merchants and Austrian Jews selling all kinds of tempting goods. The Pavlograds threw one celebration after another to mark the awards they'd earned during the campaign, and made regular trips to Olmutz to visit a certain Caroline the Hungarian, who had recently opened a restaurant there with girls as waitresses. Rostov, who had just celebrated his promotion to cornet and bought Denisov's horse Bedouin, was in debt to everyone — his comrades and the merchants alike. When he got Boris's letter, he rode to Olmutz with a fellow officer, had dinner, drank a bottle of wine, and then set off alone to the Guards' camp to find his childhood friend. He hadn't had time to get a proper uniform yet. He wore a shabby cadet jacket with a soldier's cross pinned to it, equally worn cadet riding breeches with leather patches, and an officer's saber with a sword knot. The Don horse he rode was one he'd bought from a Cossack during the campaign, and he wore a crumpled hussar cap pushed jauntily to one side. As he rode toward the camp, he imagined the impression he would make on Boris and his Guards comrades — that of a battle-hardened hussar who had actually been under fire.

The Guards had marched the whole way as if on a pleasure trip, showing off their cleanliness and discipline. They'd traveled in easy stages, their packs carried on carts, and the Austrian authorities had provided excellent dinners for the officers at every stop. The regiments had entered and left each town with bands playing, and by the Grand Duke's orders, the men had marched in perfect step the entire way — a point of pride for the Guards — with officers on foot at their proper posts. Boris had been quartered and had marched all the way with Berg, who now commanded a company. Berg had earned his captaincy during the campaign and had won his superiors' trust through his punctuality and precision. He'd also managed his finances very satisfactorily. During the campaign, Boris had made the acquaintance of several useful people and, armed with a letter of introduction from Pierre, had gotten to know Prince Andrew Bolkonsky, through whom he hoped to land a position on the commander-in-chief's staff. Berg and Boris, rested after yesterday's march, were sitting clean and neatly dressed at a round table in their tidy quarters, playing chess. Berg held a lit pipe between his knees. Boris, with his characteristic precision, was building a little pyramid of chess pieces with his slender white fingers while waiting for Berg's move, his mind clearly focused entirely on the game — as was always the case with whatever he happened to be doing.
"Well, how are you going to get out of that?" he said.
"I'll figure something out," Berg replied, touching a pawn and then pulling his hand back.
At that moment the door opened.

"Here he is at last!" Rostov shouted. "And Berg too! Oh, you little kids, go to sleep!" he exclaimed, mangling the French phrase the way his Russian nanny used to, which he and Boris had always found hilarious.
"My goodness, how you've changed!"

Boris stood up to greet Rostov, but carefully steadied some chess pieces that were about to topple over. He moved to embrace his friend, but Nicholas dodged him. With that instinct of youth — the fear of well-worn paths, the desire to express itself differently from older people who are often insincere — Nicholas wanted to do something distinctive when greeting his friend. He wanted to poke him, shove him, anything but kiss him, which was what everyone did. But Boris embraced him anyway, calmly and warmly, and kissed him three times.

They hadn't seen each other for nearly half a year, and at the age when young men are taking their first steps in life, each saw enormous changes in the other — a whole new reflection of the world they'd each entered. Both had changed drastically since their last meeting, and both were eager to show off the transformations.

"Oh, you pampered dandies! Clean and polished like you're going to a ball — not like us poor infantry sinners," Rostov cried with military swagger, his voice now carrying new baritone notes that were unfamiliar to Boris, as he pointed at his own mud-splattered breeches. The German landlady, hearing Rostov's booming voice, stuck her head through the door.
"Hey — is she pretty?" he asked with a wink.

"Why are you yelling like that? You'll scare them!" Boris said. "I wasn't expecting you today. I only sent the note yesterday through Bolkonsky — one of Kutuzov's adjutants, a friend of mine. I didn't think he'd deliver it so fast... So, how are you? Have you been under fire yet?" Boris asked.
Instead of answering, Rostov shook the soldier's Cross of St. George pinned to his jacket, indicated his bandaged arm, and looked at Berg with a smile.
"See for yourself," he said.

"Really? Well, well!" said Boris, smiling. "We've had quite a fine march ourselves, you know. His Imperial Highness rode with our regiment the entire time, so we had every comfort and advantage. The receptions we got in Poland! The dinners and balls! You wouldn't believe it. And the Tsarevich was very gracious to all the officers."
And so the two friends traded stories — one about his hussar adventures and life on the front lines, the other about the pleasures and perks of serving under members of the Imperial family.
"Oh, you Guards!" said Rostov. "Hey, send for some wine."
Boris made a face.
"If you really want it," he said.
He went to his bed, pulled a purse from under the spotless pillow, and sent for wine.
"Yes, and I have some money and a letter to give you," he added.

Rostov took the letter and, tossing the money onto the sofa, propped both arms on the table and began to read. After a few lines, he glanced angrily at Berg, then, catching his eye, hid his face behind the letter.
"Well, they've sent you a nice sum," said Berg, eyeing the heavy purse sinking into the sofa cushions. "As for us, Count, we get along on our pay. Speaking for myself..."

"Listen, Berg, my dear fellow," Rostov said, "when you get a letter from home and run into someone you've known all your life and want to pour your heart out to — and I happen to be there — I'll leave immediately so I'm not in the way. Please go somewhere, anywhere... go to hell!" he burst out, then immediately grabbed Berg by the shoulder and, looking kindly into his face to soften the harshness, added: "Don't take offense, old friend. I'm speaking from the heart, as one old acquaintance to another."
"Oh, not at all, Count! I completely understand," said Berg, getting up and speaking in his muffled, throaty voice.
"Go visit our hosts — they invited you," Boris added.

Berg put on his cleanest coat — without a single spot or speck of dust — stood before a mirror and brushed his temple hair upward in the style made fashionable by Emperor Alexander. Having satisfied himself from Rostov's glance that his coat had been noticed, he left the room with a pleased smile.
"Oh God, what a beast I am!" Rostov muttered as he read the letter.
"Why?"

"What a horrible person I am — not writing to them and giving them such a scare! What a horrible person!" he repeated, suddenly flushing. "Well, has Gabriel gone for the wine? Good — let's have some!"

Enclosed with his parents' letter was a letter of recommendation to Bagration, which the old countess had obtained through a connection at Anna Mikhaylovna's suggestion and sent along for Nicholas to deliver and make use of.
"What nonsense! As if I need this!" said Rostov, tossing the letter under the table.
"Why did you throw that away?" Boris asked.
"It's some letter of recommendation... what the hell do I need it for!"
"What do you mean, 'what the hell'?" said Boris, picking it up and reading the address. "This letter could be extremely useful to you."
"I don't need anything, and I refuse to be anyone's errand boy."
"Why not?" Boris asked.
"It's a lackey's job!"
"You're still the same dreamer, I see," Boris remarked, shaking his head.
"And you're still the same diplomat! But that's beside the point... Come on, how are things with you?" Rostov asked.
"Well, as you can see, everything's fine so far. But I'll admit I'd really like to become an adjutant rather than stay at the front."
"Why?"
"Because once a man enters military service, he should try to make the most successful career of it that he can."
"Ah, is that so?" Rostov said, clearly thinking about something else.
He stared intently and searchingly into his friend's eyes, as though trying in vain to find the answer to some question.
Old Gabriel brought in the wine.
"Should we send for Berg?" Boris asked. "He'll drink with you. I can't."
"Sure, send for him... So how do you get along with that German?" Rostov asked with a dismissive smile.
"He's a very, very nice, honest, and pleasant fellow," Boris replied.

Again Rostov studied Boris's eyes intently, then sighed. Berg came back, and the three officers' conversation grew lively over the bottle of wine. The Guardsmen told Rostov about their march and how warmly they'd been received in Russia, Poland, and abroad. They talked about the Grand Duke — his sayings and habits — and shared stories of his kindness and his terrible temper. Berg, as usual, stayed quiet whenever the subject didn't concern him, but when it came to stories about the Grand Duke's outbursts, he eagerly described how, during an inspection in Galicia, he had handled the Grand Duke's fury. With a self-satisfied smile, Berg recounted how the Grand Duke had ridden up to him in a rage, shouting "Arnauts!" — the Tsarevich's favorite word when he was furious — and demanded to see the company commander.

"Would you believe it, Count — I wasn't the least bit nervous, because I knew I was in the right. Without meaning to boast, I can say that I know the Army Regulations by heart, as well as I know the Lord's Prayer. So there's never any sloppiness in my company, and my conscience was clear. I stepped forward..." Berg stood up to demonstrate how he'd presented himself, hand at his cap, and it would have been hard to find a face expressing greater self-respect and self-satisfaction. "Well, he stormed at me — stormed and stormed and stormed! It wasn't about life so much as death, as the saying goes. 'Albanians!' and 'devils!' and 'off to Siberia!'" Berg said with a knowing smile. "I knew I was right, so I kept quiet. Wasn't that the best approach, Count? 'Hey, are you deaf?' he yelled. I still said nothing. And guess what, Count? The next day there wasn't a word about it in the daily orders. That's what keeping your head gets you. That's how it's done, Count," Berg concluded, lighting his pipe and blowing smoke rings.
"Yes, that was well done," said Rostov with a smile.

But Boris noticed Rostov was gearing up to make fun of Berg and skillfully changed the subject. He asked Rostov to tell them how and where he'd been wounded. This pleased Rostov, and he launched into the story, growing more animated as he went. He described the action at Schon Grabern the way people who've been in battle usually do — not as it actually happened, but as they wished it had, as they'd heard others describe it, as it sounded good. Rostov was an honest young man who would never tell a deliberate lie. He started out intending to describe everything exactly as it occurred, but gradually, involuntarily, inevitably, he slid into invention. If he'd told his listeners the plain truth — listeners who, like him, had heard plenty of battle stories and had a fixed idea of what a cavalry charge should sound like — they either wouldn't have believed him or, worse, would have thought Rostov himself was to blame for things not going the way such stories usually went. He couldn't just say that everyone rode forward at a trot, that he fell off his horse and sprained his arm, and then ran as fast as he could into the woods to escape a Frenchman. Besides, telling the unvarnished truth would have required a deliberate effort of will to describe only what had actually happened. Telling the truth is very hard, and young people are rarely capable of it. His listeners expected to hear how he'd been beside himself with excitement, how he'd charged the enemy like a whirlwind, cut his way through, slashing left and right, how his saber had tasted blood and he'd fallen from exhaustion. And that's what he told them.

In the middle of his story — just as he was saying, "You can't imagine what a strange frenzy comes over you during a charge" — Prince Andrew walked in. Boris had been expecting him. Prince Andrew, who enjoyed helping young men and was flattered to be asked for assistance, was well-disposed toward Boris, who had impressed him the day before, and wanted to help. Having been sent with documents from Kutuzov to the Tsarevich, he'd stopped by to see Boris, hoping to find him alone. When he entered and saw a front-line hussar holding forth about his military exploits — the type of person Prince Andrew couldn't stand — he gave Boris a friendly smile but frowned, half-closing his eyes as he looked at Rostov. He gave a slight, weary bow and sat down on the sofa with an air of languid boredom, clearly regretting that he'd walked in on such company. Rostov flushed when he noticed this, but he didn't care — this was just some stranger. Glancing at Boris, however, he could see that Boris, too, seemed embarrassed by the front-line hussar.

Despite Prince Andrew's unpleasant, mocking tone, and despite the contempt Rostov felt — from his fighting soldier's perspective — for all these little staff adjutants (which the newcomer clearly was), Rostov felt flustered. He blushed and fell silent. Boris asked what news there was from headquarters and what, without being indiscreet, one might learn about their plans.
"We'll probably advance," Bolkonsky replied, evidently reluctant to say more with a stranger present.

Berg seized the opportunity to ask, with elaborate politeness, whether it was true that the forage allowance for company captains would be doubled. Prince Andrew answered with a smile that he couldn't offer an opinion on such an important government matter, and Berg laughed delightedly.
"As for your business," Prince Andrew continued, turning to Boris, "we'll discuss it later." He glanced around at Rostov. "Come see me after the review and we'll see what can be arranged."

Then, looking around the room, Prince Andrew turned to Rostov — whose state of obvious, childish embarrassment, now giving way to anger, he didn't deign to acknowledge — and said: "I believe you were talking about the action at Schon Grabern? Were you there?"
"I was there," Rostov said aggressively, as if meaning to insult the adjutant.
Bolkonsky noticed the hussar's hostile mood, and it amused him. With a slightly condescending smile, he said: "Yes, quite a few stories are circulating about that engagement."

"Yes, stories!" Rostov repeated loudly, his eyes blazing with sudden fury as he looked from Boris to Bolkonsky. "Yes, plenty of stories! But our stories come from men who've actually been under enemy fire! Our stories carry some weight — not like the tales of staff officers who collect medals without doing a thing!"
"Is that what you think I am?" Prince Andrew asked with a calm, notably pleasant smile.
A strange mixture of rage and reluctant respect for this man's composure churned in Rostov at that moment.
"I'm not talking about you," he said. "I don't know you and, frankly, I don't want to. I'm talking about the staff in general."

"Then let me say this," Prince Andrew interrupted, his voice quiet but carrying unmistakable authority. "You clearly want to insult me, and I'll grant you it would be easy enough if you lack basic self-respect. But I'd suggest the time and place are poorly chosen. In a day or two we'll all be engaged in a far greater and more serious contest. Besides, Drubetskoy here — who says he's an old friend of yours — is hardly to blame because you find my face disagreeable. In any case," he added, rising, "you know my name and where to find me. But I want you to understand that I consider neither myself nor you insulted. And as someone older than you, my advice would be to let the whole thing drop. So then — Friday after the review, Drubetskoy, I'll be expecting you. Goodbye!" Prince Andrew bowed to them both and left.

Only after Prince Andrew was gone did Rostov think of what he should have said. And he was even angrier at himself for having failed to say it. He immediately called for his horse and, taking a cold leave of Boris, rode home. Should he ride to headquarters the next day and challenge that arrogant adjutant, or should he just let it go? This question tormented him the entire way. He thought furiously about the pleasure of seeing that small, slight, proud man's fear when facing his pistol — and then felt a surge of surprise, because of all the people he knew, there was no one he'd rather have as a friend than that very adjutant he hated so much.
